reconcile.connective: Commentators distinguish riches themselves from trusting in riches, arguing the entrance is barred not by wealth but by the idolatry it tempts — so the godly rich remain heirs of the kingdom.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells catalogs exactly these seven verses under the question "Is wealth a sign of righteousness or of wickedness?", presenting the Psalms/Proverbs prosperity texts and the Matthew/Luke/James woes as a genuine, uncollapsed contradiction.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/rich.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: not but that there have been, are, and will be, some that are rich, called by grace, brought into a Gospel church state, and are heirs of the kingdom of heaven; though these are but comparatively few: nor is it riches themselves that make the entrance so difficult, and clog the way, either into grace or glory, but putting trust and confidence in them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reframes Jesus's warning as targeting trust in wealth rather than wealth per se, allowing some rich to remain heirs of the kingdom — this is the move that reconciles the NT woes with the OT prosperity texts rather than merely explaining the verse in isolation.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 172-176
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under the heading "Worldly prosperity, a reward" / "a curse," Haley tables Psalm 112:2-3, Proverbs 15:6, Mark 10:24-25 (the Markan parallel to Matthew 19:23-24), Luke 6:20-24, Luke 12:21, and James 5:1-3 side by side, arguing righteousness only normally (not invariably) yields worldly prosperity and that the NT woes target trust in riches, not riches as such — a direct, passage-specific treatment of this contradiction.
